# Psalm 148 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

The psalm is a grand "Hallelujah Chorus" of creation. It falls into two main movements: a call for the heavens to praise (vv. 1–6) and a call for the earth to praise (vv. 7–14). Each section lists who/what should praise, then gives reasons. The psalm begins and ends with "Hallelujah" (Praise the LORD), as do all of Psalms 146–150. Spurgeon calls it "a song of nature and of grace" that "begins in the heavens, sweeps downward to dragons and all deeps, and then ascends again, till the people near unto Jehovah take up the strain."

---

## V. 1 — "Hallelujah! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places."

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist opens with a triple imperative: "Praise…Praise…Praise." Spurgeon says this is "not merely imperative, nor only hortative, but…an exultant hallelujah." He elaborates that God is to be praised *from* the heavens (as the starting point from which praise passes to other realms) and *in* the heights (adoration perfected in the heavens). "No place is too high for the praises of the most High." The word "praise" sounds nine times in the first five verses — "like minute-guns, exultant exhortations are sounded forth in tremendous force." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary notes that "Praise the LORD from the heavens" means beginning at the heavens, making them the primary source from which the praises are to be drawn. "Praise him in the heights" is rendered *in excelsis* in the Vulgate — in the most exalted regions of creation. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal) notes the psalmist considered that all heavenly beings and bodies should praise Yahweh. "The God of Israel was not a local deity who only expected honor from Israel. He was and is God over all." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

**Catholic/Patristic:** Augustine notes that the psalmist speaks "as though he had found things in heaven holding their peace in the praise of the Lord," and exhorts them to arise and praise. Yet, Augustine says, "Never have things in heaven held their peace in the praises of their Creator." The exhortation is for our sake — to stir us. "All in heaven is calm and peaceful; there is ever joy, no death, no sickness, no vexation; there the blessed ever praise God; but we are still below: yet, when we think how God is praised there, let us have our heart there." \[https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801148.htm\]

---

## V. 2 — "Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon calls angels "living intelligences, perfect in character and in bliss," and says not one bright spirit is exempted. "Whether ye be named Gabriel, or Michael…cease not, ye messengers of Jehovah, to sound forth his praise." He groups "all his hosts" as including both angelic armies and the heavenly bodies — stars, clouds, lightnings that "have their ways of praising Jehovah." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary: As angels occupy the first rank in creation and have most to praise God for, they are fitly called to commence the song. "All his host" includes beings of inferior rank to angels — "ministers of his that do his pleasure" (Ps 103:21). \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

Guzik adds that the praise of angels is the constant occupation of the living creatures surrounding God's throne (Rev 4:8), and notes that other angelic beings fell because they would not properly honor God (Isa 14:12–15). Kidner (cited by Guzik) points out that the psalm "sweeps away" the folly of worshiping angels (Col 2:18) and stars as arbiters of destiny. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

**Reformed/Desiring God (John Piper):** Piper sees here the beginning of a "praise sandwich": praising angels frame the beginning (vv. 1–2), worshiping people frame the conclusion (vv. 11–14), and sandwiched in the middle is the praise of non-volitional creation. \[https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/creation-sings-through-human-lips\]

---

## V. 3 — "Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon says the sun and moon are "paired in praise" as joint rulers of day and night. "The sun has his peculiar mode of glorifying the Great Father of lights, and the moon has her own special method of reflecting his brightness." Stars are "many, so many that no one can count the host…yet no one of them refuses to praise its Maker." He adds, "Light is song glittering before the eye instead of resounding in the ear. Stars without light would render no praise, and Christians without light rob the Lord of his glory." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary observes that sun, moon, and stars were "objects of worship to most heathen nations, but here called upon to join in the chorus of praise to God." \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

Guzik notes this is the only place in Scripture where specifically the sun, moon, and stars are bidden to praise God. Horne (cited by Guzik): "Though they have neither speech nor language…yet by their splendor and magnificence, their motions and their influences…do, in a very intelligible and striking manner, declare the glory of God." Maclaren adds: "In these starry depths obedience reigns; it is only on earth that a being lives who can and will break the merciful barriers of Jehovah's law." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

**Bible.org (Steven Cole, evangelical):** Cole notes that these inanimate things "call attention to the glory of their Creator," and suggests the heavenly bodies model worship for us: their worship is always visible, constant, and obedient. He observes that God's decree (v. 6) means the celestial bodies follow the laws of physics — "If only we were so obedient in worship!" \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 4 — "Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon interprets "heavens of heavens" as "those regions which are heavens to those who dwell in our heavens; or those most heavenly of abodes where the most choice of spirits dwell." The "waters above the heavens" are a mystery — "let them be what they may, and as they may, they shall give glory to the Lord our God." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary identifies "heavens of heavens" as the highest heavens (cf. Deut 10:14; 1 Kgs 8:27) and the "waters above the heavens" as probably the clouds (cf. Gen 1:7). \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

Kidner (cited by Guzik): "The waters above the heavens are a poetic or popular term for the rain clouds." Poole (also cited by Guzik) says "heavens of heavens" means "Ye highest and most glorious heavens, the place of God's throne and glorious presence." Adam Clarke speculated these could refer to other planets or solar systems. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

---

## V. 5 — "Let them praise the name of the LORD, for He gave the command and they were created."

**Traditional reading:** This verse shifts from imperative ("Praise!") to jussive ("Let them praise"), stating the reason. Spurgeon declares: "Evolution may be atheistic; but the doctrine of creation logically demands worship…Those who were created by command are under command to adore their Creator. The voice which said 'Let them be,' now saith 'Let them praise.'" The "name" of the LORD signifies His character, written legibly upon His works. \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary: "All creation sprang into being at the word of God (Ps 33:8)." The change of person (from "praise" to "let them praise") is "a sort of Hebrew idiom" giving liveliness and variety. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

**Bible.org:** Cole notes that "God didn't have to work hard for billions of years to create the universe. Rather, He spoke and by His infinite power, the universe came into being. Matter is *not* eternal. *God* is eternal." This stands as a key argument against theistic evolution in the commentary. \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 6 — "He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Therefore ought the Lord to be praised because he is Preserver as well as Creator, Ruler as well as Maker." The heavenly bodies are ruled by Jehovah's decree and cannot trespass against His law. "This submission to law is praise. Obedience is homage; order is harmony." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary cautions that "forever and ever" must not be pressed to imply absolute perpetuity — it means "for all time," while heaven and earth endure. The "decree which shall not pass" is compared to Gen 8:22 and Jer 31:35–36. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

**Pulpit Homilies (R. Tuck):** Tuck notes that "the permanence of natural law is not really any scientific discovery of modern date. It is the commonplace of thoughtful apprehension of facts in all ages." He distinguishes the biblical view — seeing God as the living Lawgiver behind permanence — from modern efforts "to get law separated from God." He also argues that natural laws include moral laws, and that "the moral is as natural for man as the natural is for nature." \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

**Bible.org:** Cole addresses the "new heavens and new earth" question: verse 6 does not contradict prophecies of a new creation. The new heavens and earth "will be made up of the same matter, but reconstructed and freed from the curse (Rom 8:19-22)." \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 7 — "Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon says, "The song descends to our abode, and so comes nearer home to us." "Ye dragons, and all deeps" — he says it would be idle to inquire what specific sea monsters are meant; all are intended. "About 'dragons' and 'deeps' there is somewhat of dread, but this may the more fitly become the bass of the music of the Psalm." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary: The writer "begins with the lowest parts — the deep sea, and the monsters dwelling therein." "Dragons" (or sea-monsters) refers to whales or all the greater sea-animals; "all deeps" are the extreme ocean depths. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

Ellicott notes this follows "the order of Creation in Genesis 1," beginning with sea-monsters, the "deeps" being added to include all great waters. \[Via summary in search results: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/148.htm\]

**Catholic (Haydock):** "All contribute towards the divine praise. Yet they cannot afford as much as God deserves." \[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/psalms/148.htm\]

---

## V. 8 — "lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Fire and hail. Lightning and hailstones go together. In the plagues of Egypt they cooperated in making Jehovah known in all the terrors of his power." Snow and vapours, "offsprings of cold, or creations of heat, be ye equally consecrated to his praise." Of the stormy wind he says, "Though rushing with incalculable fury, the storm wind is still under law, and moves in order due, to carry out the designs of God. It is a grand orchestra which contains such wind instruments as these!" \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary: "Fire" here is lightning, or "the various electrical phenomena accompanying storms in the East." Snow and "vapour" refers to the mist accompanying snowstorms. The stormy wind (cf. Ps 107:25) "fulfilling his word" is key — what seems uncontrolled actually obeys God. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

**Desiring God (Piper):** Piper cites this verse in an article on snow: "Snow is purposed by God to glorify him and 'do his bidding.' Snow has a Sender (Job 37:6), frost has a Scatter-er (Psalm 147:16), and God uses both to showcase his supremacy (Job 38:22)." \[https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-it-snow\]

---

## V. 9 — "mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Towering steeps and swelling knolls alike declare their Creator." He adds, "We have no longer Ebal and Gerizim, the hill of the curse and the hill of the blessing, but all our Ebals are turned to Gerizims." Fruit trees and cedars, deciduous and evergreen alike, "are equally full of benevolent design." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary, noting a possible post-exilic context, suggests the psalmist admired mountains more keenly after the flat Babylonian plains. The cedar "broke upon them as a sort of new revelation" after Babylon, which had no cedars. The vine, olive, and fig were probably in mind as "fruitful trees." \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

---

## V. 10 — "wild animals and all cattle, crawling creatures and flying birds."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon's most famous line on this verse: "Those are worse than beasts who do not praise our God. More than brutish are those who are wilfully dumb concerning their Maker." He also says, "More base than reptiles, more insignificant than insects, are songless men." The insect under the microscope and the soaring bird both "marvellously proclaim the Lord's handiwork." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

Maclaren (cited by Guzik): "The lowest worm that crawls and the light-winged bird that soars, these all have voices to praise God." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

Boice (cited by Guzik): Modern people make the mistake of worshiping creation rather than the Creator — "the psalmist reminds us that the animals themselves worship God." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

---

## V. 11 — "kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Now the poet has reached our own race, and very justly he would have rulers and subjects, chieftains and magistrates, unite in worshipping the sovereign Lord of all. Monarchs must not disdain to sing." He laments that this is not yet reality: "kings have been patrons of vice, and princes ringleaders in folly." He looks forward to the day when "through our Lord Jesus, the incarnate Wisdom, 'kings reign and princes decree justice'!" \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary: "Kings," "princes," and "judges" represent the upper classes; "peoples" or "nations" represent all the remainder. Together they include the whole human race. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

**Bible.org:** Cole notes that kings, princes, and judges "need special exhortation to praise the Lord because they tend to be enamored with their own power and glory (Calvin). As leaders, they should lead us all in praising God." \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 12 — "young men and maidens, old and young together."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Both sexes and all ages are summoned to the blessed service of song." "Old men should by their experience teach children to praise; and children by their cheerfulness should excite old men to song. There is room for every voice at this concert: fruitful trees and maidens, cedars and young men, angels and children, old men and judges — all may unite in this oratorio." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

Maclaren (cited by Guzik): "The young man's strong bass, the maiden's clear alto, the old man's quavering notes, the child's fresh treble, should blend in the song." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

Kidner (cited by Cole): "In these few lines there emerges, quite incidentally and with unforced simplicity, the only potential bond between the extremes of mankind: a joyful preoccupation with God." \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 13 — "Let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "His unique name should have a monopoly of praise." "He is himself the crown of all things, the excellency of the creation. There is more glory in him personally than in all his works united. It is not possible for us to exceed and become extravagant in the Lord's praise: his own natural glory is infinitely greater than any glory which we can render to him." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

Ellicott notes a "fine artistic touch" in the word order: all heaven and earth have been summoned to the chorus of praise, of Him who is now declared to be *above* earth and heaven. \[Search excerpt from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/148.htm\]

VanGemeren (cited by Guzik) points out that "Let them praise" is in the jussive (command) form: "the psalmist restates the universal obligation of all of God's creation to demonstrate their allegiance by praising him." \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

**Bible.org (Kidner comparison):** Kidner contrasts the worship of the heavens (v. 5: "For he commanded and they were created" — existence-praise) with the worship of people (v. 13: "For his name…is exalted" — conscious praise based on revelation). "God's glory in the natural world is the reign of law (v. 6)…but among His people His glory is redemptive love (v. 14)." \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

---

## V. 14 — "He has raised up a horn for His people, the praise of all His saints, of Israel, a people near to Him. Hallelujah!"

**Traditional reading:** This is the climax. Spurgeon explains the "horn" as strength, fame, and victory: "When they are brought low he raises up a horn for them by sending them a deliverer; when they are in conflict he gives them courage and strength…and when all is peaceful around them, he fills their horn with plenty." He notes the mutual relationship: "He lifts up their horn, and they lift up his praise. He exalts them, and they exalt him." For "a people near unto him," Spurgeon says this is "near by kin, and near by care; near as to manifestation and near as to affection…true even more emphatically of the spiritual Israel, the believing seed." \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

The Pulpit Commentary discusses a textual ambiguity: some take "praise" in apposition with "horn" (God exalts their horn and their praise), others translate "Praise belongs to all his saints" (Kay) or "Seemly is praise for all his saints" (Cheyne). "A people near unto him" draws on covenant language (Deut 4:7). \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-148.html\]

Ellicott: "The raising of the horn evidently implies some victory, or assurance of victory, which, no doubt, gave the first impulse for this song of praise." He addresses the charge that this verse "narrows a grand universal anthem" by arguing that "while poetically all the universe…can be called to sing 'hallelujah,' it remains as it has ever been, the covenant privilege of Israel." \[Search excerpt\]

**Reformed/Desiring God (Piper):** Piper emphasizes that the psalm "ends with a specific call to God's people to praise." He sees the whole psalm as ultimately about human praise: "every single command to worship for the stars and whales and storm clouds…is a new command for us to joyfully worship the Creator." When we behold God's attributes in creation, "at that moment his creation is praising him through us." \[https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/creation-sings-through-human-lips\]

**Bible.org:** Cole identifies the "horn" prophetically with Christ: "As Luke 1:69 declares, the Lord God of Israel 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David His servant.'" He describes God's people under four titles from this verse: (1) His people — chosen and redeemed; (2) His godly ones — set apart; (3) sons of Israel — heirs of covenant promises; (4) a people near to Him — brought near by Christ's blood (Eph 2:13). "That is the climax of the psalm, as it is of the gospel: 'Behold, the dwelling of God is with men' (Rev 21:3)." \[https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-148-let-heaven-and-earth-praise-lord\]

**Catholic (Haydock):** Notes that "horn" can mean "glory, or the Messias; though this cannot easily be proved to be the literal sense." The "saints" are the Israelites, "particularly the sacred ministers" (Deut 4:7). \[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/psalms/148.htm\]

**Catholic/Patristic (Augustine):** Augustine interprets "the horn of His people" in light of Haggai and Zechariah: "Now the horn of His people is humble in afflictions, in tribulations, in temptations, in beating of the breast; when will He exalt the horn of His people? When the Lord has [come]…" He sees the confession of all creation — heaven and earth alike — as their voice of praise. \[https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801148.htm\]

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**The main interpretive differences on Psalm 148 are not large between Protestant traditions.** All major traditions read it as a universal call to praise. Differences emerge in emphasis:

- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Emphasizes sovereign grace in v. 14 — "he is good to all, but he is God to his people." The "children of Israel" apply "even more emphatically to the spiritual Israel, the believing seed." Strong creationist stance (v. 5: "Evolution may be atheistic…"). \[https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps148.php\]

- **Reformed Baptist / Christian Hedonist (Piper, Desiring God):** Reads the psalm through the lens of human joy in God. Creation's praise is ultimately *human* praise offered in response to creation's witness. The psalm points toward the supremacy of God in all things for the joy of all peoples. \[https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/creation-sings-through-human-lips\]

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Stresses that the call to praise is not an empty wish but a prophecy fulfilled in Revelation 5:11–13. Emphasizes the "command" nature of the jussive verbs — all creation has an *obligation* to praise. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-148/\]

- **Post-exilic/historical reading (Pulpit, Cambridge):** The Pulpit Commentary and Cambridge Bible tie the psalm to Israel's restoration after exile, reading v. 14 as the clue: "Israel, rejoicing in the restoration of its national existence, calls heaven and earth to join in a diapason of praise." This historical-critical nuance is more pronounced in older Anglican/mainline scholarship.

**I could not locate specific Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary on this psalm within the search and fetch limits available.**

---

## Other Views

**Catholic/Patristic (Augustine, Haydock):** Augustine's reading is deeply Christological and eschatological. He connects the "Hallelujah" of Psalm 148 to the Easter season — the time *after* the Resurrection signifies the bliss of the life to come. The "horn" is read in connection with Haggai and Zechariah's prophecies. Augustine stresses that praise must involve the whole self: "let not your tongue and voice alone praise God, but your conscience also, your life, your deeds." The Haydock commentary adds a Marian/ecclesial note: the "horn" relates to God "establishing his Church." \[https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801148.htm\] \[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/psalms/148.htm\]

**Modern scholarship:** I was unable to retrieve content from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the available search/fetch limits. The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges (partially available in search results) represents a moderately critical approach: it ties the psalm to post-exilic restoration, notes its liturgical use, and observes that it "implies the significance of Israel's history for the history of the world, and, in view of the unity of all being, for the history of the universe." It should be read in connection with Romans 8:19ff and Revelation 5:13. The germ of the psalm is found in Nehemiah 9:5–6, and the *Benedicite* (Song of the Three Holy Children) is based on it. \[Search excerpt from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/148.htm\]
